name: voracious_radix_sort (MSD/LSD radix sorts)
verdict_reason: On large integer arrays the radix sorts beat the std sorts of their time by about 3x (unstable) to 5x (stable) on u64. The baseline was pre-1.81 std; ipnsort and driftsort narrow the gap, though the ipnsort authors still expect radix sorts to win on small integer types. Below about 1,000 elements there is no gain.
tier_reason: First-party results files with the CPU named, but no rustc version or flags for the run and no independent reproduction.
claimed_speedup: u64, 1,000,000 uniform values: 11.94 ns per item vs 37.39 for sort_unstable and 58.89 for sort (about 3.1x and 4.9x, derived from page data); 100 values: 27.12 vs 26.25 ns per item (no gain).
workload: Single-threaded sort of u64 arrays from 100 to 10,000,000 elements across uniform, small-range, sorted and other distributions, 5 iterations each.
platforms: All Rust targets; multithreaded variants use rayon
one_liner: Radix sorts for Rust primitives and keyed structs; about 3x faster than pre-1.81 sort_unstable on a million u64.
how_it_is_fast: Radix sorts place elements by the bits of their key instead of comparing them, doing a fixed number of linear passes per byte of key. The crate picks among MSD, LSD and hybrid variants by type and length and falls back to std sorts for small inputs.
use_it_when: Sorting large arrays (roughly 10^4 elements or more) of integers, floats or structs with an integer key.
skip_it_when: Short arrays: it falls back to std sorts, and below about 1,000 elements the results show no gain.
Comparison-defined orders or strings, which it does not support.
Memory is tight: some variants use up to 2x the array size.
caveats: The baseline std sorts in these results predate Rust 1.81's ipnsort and driftsort; no newer comparison was found.
Tuning constants were profiled on the author's Ryzen 3950X and may not fit other CPUs.
No rustc version or optimization flags are stated for the 1.2.0 results; the README's last tested toolchain is Rust 1.46.
tradeoffs: Out-of-place variants allocate up to the array size again.
Sorting custom types requires implementing the crate's Radixable trait.
